title: Creating a Culture of Accountability
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article defines accountability as accepting the obligation for a specific outcome and owning the result, quoting the line that it is the glue tying commitment to the result. It argues that the strongest form of accountability in a culture is carried by peers rather than leaders, with everyone expected to speak openly and candidly about any lack of commitment or sub-par performance. Contrary to expectation, the author says this does not create a confrontational climate but makes relationships more caring and stronger, because great teams refuse to let each other down. The prescribed move is for leaders to model the standard first, being open and candid with each other and accepting frank assessment of their own performance, and then to extend that expectation to every team member. The piece ends with the claim that accountability and culture are destiny for organizations.
points: Accountability means accepting the obligation for an outcome and owning the result, which ties commitment to performance.
In a mature accountability culture, peers rather than leaders carry the strongest flame by calling out lapses openly.
Mutual candor strengthens relationships rather than producing a confrontational climate.
Leaders must first model frank assessment of all performance, including their own, before the expectation can spread to everyone.
quotes: When a team member or leader accepts the obligation of achieving a specific outcome, they become accountable. By owning the result, they commit to perform and to achieve the desired end state. In the words of one leadership expert, “Accountability is the glue that ties commitment to the result.
In a culture replete with accountability, every team member feels some ownership and responsibility for the larger results. More importantly, they feel accountable to each other.

When accountability pervades a culture, it isn’t leaders who carry the strongest flame, but peers. Organizations that expect peers to engage openly and candidly about any and all performance unleash a tornado of personal responsibility.

When everyone knows they are expected to call others out when they observe any lack of commitment or sub-par performance, the entire organization of team members becomes accountable to each other. Surprisingly to some, this doesn’t produce a negative work climate or a highly confrontational atmosphere.

Quite the contrary. When everyone is truly accountable to each other, relationships become deeply caring and get even stronger. It is often said that great teams are made up of members who refuse to let each other down.

Once leaders demonstrate with their own actions that they will tolerate nothing less than frank and honest assessments of all performance, including their own, a culture of accountability has a great chance to emerge. For organizations, accountability and culture are destiny.
